utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning, sound engineers; good morning, interpreters. I trust you're there. Yes, they are. Good morning, counsel for the Prosecution, for the Defence. General Krstic, good morning. We are back here to resume our case. The difference from yesterday is that Judge Riad has joined us again, and I should like to greet him back. We have also taken -- we have to take a decision today with regard to the matter raised yesterday, and that decision will be pronounced verbally, that is, yesterday, but the Prosecutor asked to tender into evidence certain exhibits, that is, 14, 17, and 18, to which the Defence objected, claiming that they related to Nova Kasaba and the Jadar River. Those are places not indicated in paragraphs 24 to 26 of the indictment. In fact, the paragraph 24 of the indictment says that between the 11th and the 18th of July, the executions of the Muslims in Bosnia were mass executions and that they took place in Srebrenica and its environs; that is, the places which are then listed. The expression used here is clearly indicative of this list as an example rather than the exhaustive list of places mentioned here. Beyond this, the principles of the material truth which govern criminal law, and in particular international criminal law, require that truth and the whole truth be established while respecting the rights of the accused. Therefore, there are no violations of the rights of the accused, because the accused knew of these places, owing to the fact that the Prosecution had disclosed documents to the Defence. The Chamber, therefore, has decided to admit all of the exhibits that were tendered by the Prosecution, including Exhibits 14, 17, and 18. So this is the decision of the Chamber. I should like to ask the registrar, Mr. Dubuisson, to take note of this decision and do whatever is necessary in this respect. So this is the decision of the Chamber. Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Do you wish to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, will the decision be also taken in writing or is this the final decision, the verbal decision, as you have just pronounced it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should take it as the verbal decision which was taken. We have not made the decision in writing, so preferably we shall take our decisions in this manner unless, exceptionally, there are certain reasons when, for instance, a motion or objection is submitted in writing, in which case the Chamber will respond in writing. But this is the final decision, and that is why I drew the attention of the Registry to take note of this decision. There will be no decision in writing. This is the decision of the Chamber. Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. So the witness, whom we were hearing yesterday, can resume his testimony, and I, therefore, give the floor to Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Then we would ask that protected Witness B come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Can you hear me? Good morning. I should like to remind you that you are still under oath and you will now answer further questions that Mr. McCloskey will have to ask of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the translation in Serbo-Croatian, so I don't think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You probably want to change it to channel 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You may have heard, as the tape was being played, that General Mladic made a reference to who actually invited who to the meeting. What is your recollection about who called the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my recollection, the battalion Commander was ordered to go to Fontana, so I think that Mladic ordered to come there. So he organised the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he also -- General Mladic also, and I'll refer to Exhibit 39A, the transcript, he states on the bottom of the page 15: "And you've isolated our people, especially that guy of yours Van den Broek. He's one of those who have destroyed the dream of a state both to us and the Muslims. Sir, we were a happy country and happy peoples, and we had a good life both in Srebrenica and here until the Muslims began to listen to Van den Broek, Zimmerman, Kohl, and similar Western Mafia were telling them." Who was Van den Broek at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time Van den Broek was the Minister of Foreign Affairs in Holland, and he was several times also by the soldiers we had contact with -- Jovo's accused that he was one of the men who arranged what was going on and was for the Muslims and against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And during that meeting, you can be seen standing there near Mladic, next to Colonel Karremans. How did you feel during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very uncomfortable, because when I saw the tape, I think I missed some parts of the tape, and in my opinion and in my notes I can find that he threatened us that when there would be airstrikes again on his, say, soldiers, then he would start shooting at the compound and at the refugees, and also our hostages could be targets, the hostages in Bratunac. After he started screaming to Colonel Karremans and accusing him of asking for the airstrikes, after that he did the same to me and after that he did the same to Major Boering. In the first ten minutes I was very uncomfortable, and I had the idea that it was possible that we would be brought out and be shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the meeting ended with another meeting planned. Can you tell us what happened after the meeting ended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the meeting ended we just visited for a few minutes our soldiers. I think we were allowed to be there five minutes. After that we were let out of the hotel. We went back to the compound in Potocari and had to find a representative, and after talking with men or women we knew and we had seen in the refugees -- in or outside the compound, we found out that Mr. Mandzic was there, and we knew Mr. Mandzic, because we visited him several times at the secondary school in Srebrenica. And then we thought it would be a good representative if he would like to do it for us. And we asked him and, well, he was free to go with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 2300 hours we went back to the Hotel Fontana for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, Mr. Karremans, myself and Mr. Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you escorted back to the hotel by anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I think that we were escorted from Jovo's place to the hotel. Well, I'm not sure, but I think it was Nikolic again, but I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you got to the hotel, who was there at this second meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wrote it down in my notes. General Mladic was there; Nikolic was there, Major Nikolic; Colonel Jankovic; somebody who was called a representative of the Drina Corps. Later on it seemed that it was the General Krstic. Kosoric was there, the film team was there, and a lot of civilians, and one of them was Ljubisav Simic. It was a name which was mentioned sometime before by Jovo. He was announced as the mayor of Bratunac. And during that meeting we discovered that he was a former colleague from Mr. Mandzic, so that's why I know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the person who your notes indicate was a representative of the Drina Corps. Do your notes or does your memory indicate getting a name or a rank of that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in my notes; only as a representative of the Drina Corps in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you ever seen that person before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you later see him on television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when he was arrested inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you sure that that's the same person --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure that's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you see that person that was introduced to you as a representative of the Drina Corps present in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's sitting over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you point out what he's wearing so we know who you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the guard but the man sitting with the headphones on his head, in I think a blue or a grey jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Will the record indicate he's identified the defendant, General Krstic. Now, who was leading the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic was leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the first thing you remember occurring at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we took a seat, and after that somebody opened the window and the curtains from the room we were sitting in, and a pig was slaughtered under the window. It screamed terrible, and I think it was just to intimidate us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long did this pig scream for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to say now, but maybe two, maybe three minutes. But in that situation it's hard, very difficult, to know the exact time. I wrote it down in my notes. We were there at 2300 hours, and at 5 minutes past 11.00 in the evening, the slaughtering of the pig started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened after the pig stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the pig stopped, they closed the window. A lot of them, of the Serbs who were in the room, were just smiling. The window was closed, the curtain was closed, and we started with the meeting, in which Mladic started to tell us that he did not find any medicines in Srebrenica. When he arrived in the hospital, all the medicines were gone. That was the first item.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the last several months have you had a chance to see a partial video of that second meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen a small part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that help refresh your recollection as to who was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen -- there was General Krstic, which I didn't remember by name, but after seeing him on television in 1998, I knew his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was he seated at that second meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the left side of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the next subject that was discussed, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I found my notes from that meeting at 15 minutes past 11.00. Mladic showed us a board that he took from the opstina in Srebrenica. He showed as a trophy and I think he told us that Srebrenica was his town now. After that he had a talk with Mr. Mandzic, and it was very difficult for me to follow that speech, because they were sitting rather next to each other. Petar was interpreting for the Colonel Karremans and there were, I think, two persons sitting between them and myself, so I just picked up some things. It was a rather relaxed talk, and Mladic explained to Mandzic that the population had to choose and had to say who wants to go where when they left the enclave. It was also possible to stay, but I don't think it was a real option.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you had a difficult time hearing the translation --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- because of where you were seated? And about how long did that meeting last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted till about 12.00 in the evening. After the talk with Mandzic, Mladic told that he was able to arrange buses to transport the people where they wanted to go. At 20 minutes past 11.00 there was a statement from Mandzic, and I don't know, because it was in Serbo-Croatian and I didn't get the translation exactly what he said, but it was a rather calm talk. After that there was a statement from General Mladic, in which I could hear also from -- parts from the translation that he was accusing Mandzic and the Muslims for what they have done, going out of the enclave, killing Serb people outside the enclave. He was looking very mean and it was a very tense moment again. At that same meeting we had talks about food for the refugees, eventual Medevacs for the wounded which were on the compound, maybe bringing in food by UNHCR, providing diesel for the buses and the trucks, who would do it and if there were possibilities. Well, we had no logistic convoy, so we couldn't provide it, but I think that they said there would be a convoy. There was a discussion about the buses and I think we tried to find a time schedule, but there were no details in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There were no details to what in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: A time schedule, who would provide the buses, who would provide the diesel. Well, it was just -- it had to be arranged, but nobody said, well, you will do this and I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there any indication it would happen the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just that it would happen and there would be buses somewhere and some when, but not when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was anything specifically planned for the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A new meeting at 10.00, because Mladic ordered Mandzic to go back and see where the population wanted to go, and he had to come back the next morning at 10.00 for a new meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Mladic say anything about the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He tried several times to inform Colonel Karremans that he needed a contact with the military leaders from the Muslims. He wanted that they would surrender, hand over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the BSA, he promised that there would be a ceasefire up till 10.00 the next morning, so 10.00 on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that most of what you recall about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened after the meeting ended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting ended, we went back to the compound in Potocari, and I don't know if we did it, but I think that Mr. Mandzic did it. He found two other representatives from the population, Camila and Ibro Nuhanovic, who would support him. Colonel Karremans made his report. That's what he told us and sent his reports to north-east command, his higher echelon, and I think also to Sarajevo, to BH Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then did you -- where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spend the night in the compound in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened in the morning of July 12th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the morning we first had a meeting with the representatives of the civilian population. They wanted to inform Mr. Mulatovic, Izetbegovic, and Silajdzic. That's what they told. They tried to use our telephone, but they had a big problem to get in contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who were those individuals they wanted to inform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the Muslim representatives in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the government. At the same moment we tried to talk about creating safe zones for the refugees, where they could stay, because we didn't know how long they had to stay there, and about some home rules that had to be made, because there were a lot of refugees on the compound and outside the compound, and we had to arrange something. Now, that was a small problem because at 9.00, although it was a promise that there would be a ceasefire till 10.00, at three minutes past nine, a round from a tank hit one of the houses at the OP site opposite side of the compound. After that, several tank rounds for the next ten --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. After that, the first round at three minutes past nine, in the next ten minutes several rounds hit the houses at the OP site, opposite side of the compound. I had to do some other jobs inside the compound. We started with destroying some information we had from which we thought that it was not good that the Serbs get it in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you think the Serbs might get it in their hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at the same moment, at 9.00, when the rounds hit the houses, the Serbs entered -- and I can show it on the map -- from OP Papa, from the north in Potocari, at the east and west side of the road. They went southwards in the direction of the compound. So a big group of Serb soldiers came in the vicinity of the compound, and we did not know what they wanted to do, if they would come on the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to you see them enter the area with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I seen them enter the area. They split up and came in a very bright front forward to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, between 9.00 and 10.00, I think, they walked forward burning haystacks. I think they did it so they could see where they had to stay on the line and go forward all together. There were groups with dogs with them walking through the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many dogs did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw five or six groups with dogs. A group of five or six men with a dog.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing happened. They just walked around the compound at the east and the west side. They did not enter the compound, did not go to the refugees in the factories south of the compound, and just stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell how the refugees reacted when the Serb soldiers appeared on the scene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course when the first tank rounds landed in the houses, there was a lot of screaming and a lot of anxious people all over the place, of course. And, of course, when the Serb soldiers came closer to the refugees, they were very anxious. But I wasn't in the factories at the moment. I stayed inside the compound because I had a lot of other things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The third meeting was scheduled to be held at --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 10.00. Well, I know -- I don't know when they left, but I know that the three representatives of the civilian population, Major Boering, and Karremans went to Fontana again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why didn't you go this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had to do some other things. Emergency sorting inside the compound and somebody had to do that, so I couldn't go with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what significant things happened that morning, after 10.00, that you were able to experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically on the compound. I know that Karremans, Major Boering, and representatives came back after the meeting. They had talked about fuel, buses, time schedule. That's what I thought, but again there was no concrete deal over what would happen. So the Colonel Karremans ordered Major Boering and myself to go back to Fontana and try to find out how the situation with the fuel should be arranged and how many buses would be provided by Mladic and the time schedule, when what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us: At that point, was there an anticipation or information that it would happen that very day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because they came back from that meeting, and I think they still had no idea when it would happen. And that has been confirmed, because at 12.00 I went with Major Boering back to the Hotel Fontana to find out what I just told you and nobody was there. Well, a lot of soldiers, but no representatives we could deal with. And I think that somebody in the hotel phoned for the Major Nikolic, which we asked for, and Major Nikolic showed up with Kosoric. We had a small talk outside -- or in the lobby of the hotel, and suddenly they told us we had to go back because the buses were already there and they would start the evacuation. Well, we were very surprised and went back, I think about 1.00, to Potocari. When we arrived there were already, I think, 15 buses standing in front of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you had left the compound that morning, were there any vehicles, buses, or trucks along the road between the compound and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that there was any vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that an area that was cordoned off by you before you were taken over by the Serbs, the roadway between the UN base and OP Papa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that moment again, but we had the OP Papa, and then, of course, that was at the entrance of the enclave. So that was cut off till the moment that the Serbs enter the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you had left to go to the hotel that morning, had the Serbs already entered the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But -- and we had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I'm sorry that I have to interrupt you, but I do not think that at this speed we can really do our work. The interpreters are following you only with very great difficulty. Witness, you must be aware of the existence of interpreters. You already had some experience. You've worked with interpreters. Mr. McCloskey, you should establish the pace. If you make a break, if you make a pause, and if you speak slowly, then, I believe, the witness will do the same. I am sorry for having to interrupt you, but it is in the interests of work and in the interests of justice. When a witness says things that are very important, then we really have to follow him and understand him. If he goes too fast, we simply miss some of this information. So will you please speak slowly, as I do now, with pauses so that the interpreters can follow us. Right. Very well. I'm quite sure that you can do it. Please go on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if I can remember where I was. I'm sorry. I was asking you buses and the enclave when you went to Bratunac. Again, you said there were no buses in the enclave area when you went to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left -- I think it was 12.00 -- there were no buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you came back at 1.00, there were buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we came back, I think there were 15 buses standing in front of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was the -- what was the next thing that happened when you got back that afternoon and saw these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- I think the first thing we did, entered the compound, report to Colonel Karremans what happened to us. After that we went outside because we had the indication that evacuation or deportation started. People were led into the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went out and I saw that people were led into the buses from the area where they were assembled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe that process as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, the refugees were deadly afraid. They saw the buses and that was for them the indication, "Well, they bring us to a safer place. So let's go as quick to the buses, go as fast as possible to the buses," and, "I will be first."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was talk in the buses. First, the wounded. Well, it was the request of Mr. Mandzic, first the wounded and then elderly people and women. After that the rest would be evacuated. Well, at that moment, everybody was able to stand up, pick up his luggage, went to the buses, and they overcrowded the buses. We tried to arrange, at that moment, to put an UN soldier in each bus to accompany and escort them, but that was not possible because the buses were too overcrowded. At that moment, Major Boering and Captain Voerman were ordered to take a jeep and escort the buses to where wherever they would go, and we heard that they went to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there any separation of the men at that early stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember if it happened with the first few buses that there was already a separation. I think that at the end of filling up the buses, the first separation started. When men went forward to go to the buses, they were separated and brought to the White House near the entrance of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe that process as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly at what moment it started, but I think when the first buses were there; otherwise, for sure when the second buses -- group of buses was there. The people were able to go forward to the buses. Everybody tried to go, most of them they went to the right side of the bus. I don't know why the right side, but it just happened. But at that moment, the Serb soldiers started to pick out of the refugees the men, I think from the age from 17 up to 70 years old and led them to the White House near the entrance of the compound. They told us that they had to do that because they wanted to find out if they were soldiers and if they were in the army during the war. If they were in the army, they would be separated, be made prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did some of these men have property?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Everybody who could carry something had his property with him, as far as they could take it, but the women and children and elderly men who were brought to the buses were able to take the property inside the buses, most of it, and the men who were brought to the White House had to leave their luggage outside of the house and were brought, without any luggage, inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to the men after they went to the White House?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they first stayed for an interrogation inside the house. Outside I talked with General Mladic, who showed up that afternoon. I asked what was going on with the men who were separated and who were brought into the house, and he told me that -- and tried to find out if there were soldiers among them, and if it was so, they would be separated, be made prisoners of war, brought to a prison camp in the vicinity of Bijeljina and exchanged for Serb prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what time General Mladic arrived in the area of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was somewhere in the afternoon. I think in the middle of the afternoon, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see -- when did you first see men separated and put on buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the first. I think 15 buses, if it already happened, because I am for sure in those bus there were some men, but at the same moment or shortly after it, the separation started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you see? Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, men would like to go with their families into the buses. They just were separated, led to the White House. They had to leave their luggage outside and were brought in the White House. I think at the second part of that afternoon, at least three buses of men were filled up in front of the White House, and they were brought in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it myself. When they left, one of our vehicles with Versteeg, I mentioned his name also yesterday, they escorted the buses in the direction of Bratunac. Later on, I heard in Bratunac the UN vehicle was stopped and was not able to escort the buses further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever -- how did the Serb soldiers do this separation process? Was it friendly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that during the separation they used force, because the men who were separated just did what they had to do and they listen to the Serb soldiers. When they came out of the White House, I seen several times that the men were very afraid, tried to escape, started screaming, did not want to go into the buses. At that moment, some force was used. They were hit and kicked into the buses. When they were in the buses and they tried to get out of the bus, you can see from the entrance of our compound that they were ordered to sit in the bus with their head down so that they could not see what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That afternoon of the 12th, did you recognise any other Serb soldiers besides General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic was always around and a lot of other Serb soldiers, but none of them I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see General Krstic there that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to make out particular units from insignia or from anything else about, you know, what kind of Serb units these were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I had the idea that the Serb units who entered the enclave were normal Serb units. During that afternoon, I heard that some of our vehicles were captured on the road to Kladanj by non-regular troops in several uniforms, civilian clothes, some in black overalls, but I didn't recognise any specific ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During this process in the afternoon when people are taken to the White House and people are put on buses, did you hear any gunfire in the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I just ask. He used the word "Serb units." Does he mean the units from the Serb army or Bosnian Serb units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever have any indication that there were Serb units from Serbia involved in this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only information we got, when the enclave was still in our hands, that some units of Arkan were in the vicinity, but I've never seen them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you, that afternoon while this was happening, hear any gunfire in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we heard all the time gunfire. The units who spread up in the northern part and marched forward to the south were all over the place and we heard all the time gunfire from the mountains surrounding the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell whether there was gunfire coming from the area around the factories and the compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically in the area from the compound or the factories, just in the hills which were around it, and it's very difficult when you hear gunfire, to point it out, where it's coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did the Serb soldiers react to the gunfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the same as we did. We got used to it. We had the idea that we were no targets, so it just happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What else happened that afternoon? What else were you involved in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went out several times to go to the refugees outside in the factories. Once there was the interpreter of the Bravo Company, Mr. Hodzic. I don't know exactly, but there is a story that one of the bodyguards of Mladic took his ID card, and I think that I took it back from him, and he was so afraid that I had to bring him back to the compound. It was not possible for me to use him as an interpreter to talk to the refugees. After that, I went out with one of the representatives, Ibro Nuhanovic, to go to the refugees, and when we left the front gate of the compound, suddenly a Serb soldier came to him and started beating him in his face. I was able to stop it and after that we returned to the compound, because it was not safe to take him to the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ibro Nuhanovic was one of the representatives that had gone to the Hotel Fontana that morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And in the same meeting General Mladic promised safety for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you have a meeting with Mr. Nuhanovic and other representatives that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the afternoon we had a meeting with the representatives, and several subjects were discussed. Of course there was a lot of panic because it started so quick, and the representatives told us that although there was a deal that first the wounded, then the elderly, and then the sick people, and then women and children would be evacuated, now they saw there was a mix-up, and not only a mix-up from all those groups, but also that men were separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did the representatives -- what did the representatives think of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had a very bad feeling about it, because they referred to what happened in 1992 and 1993, when also a lot of men were separated and brought to a soccer field in Bratunac and were killed over there, and they thought that this would happen again. Well, we could only promise, of course, that we would try to monitor it and escort the vehicles, but they told us that, well, we had no choice and the UN was not able to protect them, because the UN was not arranging anything; General Mladic was ordering what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I notice you looked at your notes when you said that. Did you take notes at that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have a lot of notes from that meeting, because they were very concerned and had a lot of subjects which they would like to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what else did they talk about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't agree with the sequence from the evacuation. They had no choice -- we had no choice again, because Mladic was arranging things, and not the UN. They requested us to phone to Tuzla to see if things were arranged over there. When the refugees went to Kladanj, after that they should be brought to Tuzla, and of course they wanted to know what happened in Tuzla. They ordered us to inform the refugees over what's going on now, what will happen the coming hours, or maybe days, inform them what was arranged with Mladic, tell them that he said there was safety and security for them, and try to avoid that there was panic among the refugees. But of course they were very afraid, so that was very difficult. They asked us to report to the world what was going on, and of course we told them that all the things we saw and what was happening was reported to our higher echelons. Mr. Nuhanovic told us that he agreed to go to the meeting that morning because he wanted to do something for his people and also for the battalion, but at that specific moment he had the idea that he was doing a dirty job, because it was no longer the UN who arranged things, but the Serbs did. And after the meeting that morning, because nothing was really arranged, the evacuation should not have started. He told us that when he had known that there were cameras, then he did not -- he wouldn't have gone over there. When things were going on in the way they did now, men would try to escape and flee into the woods. Mr. Mandzic had a contact with the representatives of the BH government in Central Bosnia, and I don't know with whom, but he told us that they informed him that they should not let go buses or evacuations going on without a UN escort. And again they told us that Mladic promised and guaranteed security for all of them, but they had their doubts about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And after that meeting did the separations and transportation continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it continued, I think, till 8.00 in the evening. Also at the end of that afternoon, there should be a medical evacuation to Kladanj. Fifty-four, that's what's in my notes, persons wounded were let into the buses or into trucks and brought to Kladanj. Some of them, and I don't know, but I think it was about 20 people, were able to leave the buses in Kladanj and go by foot across the border. The rest of them were not able to go there by themselves, so they stayed in the buses and in the trucks and went back with one of our escorts to Bratunac, to the checkpoint with Jovo's. They were not allowed to go to the hospital in Bratunac or the hospital in our compound; they had to stay at Yellow Bridge, and I'm for sure that I got the information that night that one of the wounded died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Anything else of significance that you recall occurring before you -- before the evening ended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is all I have in my notes from the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the morning of the 13th, can you describe to us what occurred on the 13th, from your memory and your notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that between 7.00 and 8.00 in the morning, the evacuation started again. That morning we got the information from the Lieutenant de Ruiter that he found nine dead bodies in the vicinity of the compound, all shot, all with a hole in the back, so he thought it was an execution. Of course he could not prove that, but he went there with Lieutenant Koster. Lieutenant Koster sat down between the dead bodies and de Ruiter took a picture. After that they tried to get back to the refugees where they had to stay. They were seen by a Serb soldier and they told me that somebody shot at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That night in the compound, as you were sleeping, the night of the 12th/early morning hours of the 13th, did you hear any gun fire in the vicinity of the compound or the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, the gun fire was still going on and we were so used to it that we didn't hear specifically that it was in an other way than we were used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After the report of the bodies by de Ruiter what was the next thing that occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my notes I see that General Mladic was again present in the morning and he had a contact with Colonel Karremans. I wasn't at that meeting, so I don't know what they talked about. And that same morning I had a small talk with General Mladic about the theft from weapons and materiel by the Serb soldiers from our soldiers, and asked to get all those things, weapons and flak jackets, back from them. Well, he promised me that of course at this moment it was a problem, but he should order his soldiers to stop and not steal anything from the UN soldiers. At that same time he told me that fights were going on in the north-western part of the enclave, and that was one thing we knew already, because when the refugees were brought from Bratunac to Kladanj via this road, we heard that lots of fightings were going on on this road. And when Mladic told us that fights were going on in the north-western part of the enclave, it was nothing amazing for us. He told me that we had to inform the Muslim army that they had to stop and surrender and to hand over their weapons, because a lot of them were killed and also a lot of Serb soldiers were killed, and it would be good for us to inform the Muslims to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any other VRS soldiers or officers that you recognised around that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, Mladic with his bodyguards, and Jankovic, he was all the time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you see Jankovic on the 13th also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because a lot of vehicles were stolen on the road from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje and Kladanj, it was not possible to escort all the transports, so somebody, and I think that Major Franken or Colonel Karremans, took the decision to create four mobile checkpoints on the road to see if the buses passed and so that they had at least something to inform us what happened on that road. That same day, I think in the second part of the morning, between 10.00 and 11.00, Colonel Akamovic showed up. He told us that he was a logistic officer and told us that we would get a logistical convoy. It would be able to bring in 15.000 litres of water, 36.000 litres of diesel, and 20.000 rations. At the same moment he told us that from the 36.000 litres of diesel, we had to give some of it to the Serbs. We had to share it together, because they provided up till that moment the diesel for the evacuation buses and trucks. And maybe I jump further on. At the end of the day I know that a convoy arrived, that there was diesel in it. And Major Franken and Colonel Jankovic made the deal, and I don't know exactly, but I know that 30.000 litres of our diesel went to the BSA in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that occur on the end of the day of the 13th or on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It arrived on the 14th, and on the 14th they supported the BSA with the diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the fuel arrived the next day after your meeting --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- with Acamovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Acamovic told us that there should be made a list from all the personnel, from the local staff, the UNHCR, the MSF, which would stay with us and leave with us in the enclave. So we made a list with names: first names, male or female, date of birth, and since when they worked for the UN that day. That same morning, outside the compound, I've seen that Mr. Kingori, one of the UNMOs, had a lot of talks with Colonel Jankovic outside, because he got the information and also was able to go into the White House to see that it was overcrowded. It was again a very hot day, so all the days at that moment, and it was a very bad situation in the White House. So Kingori decided to ask Jankovic to provide some buses and transport some men from the White House to create a better situation, because it was very bad at that moment. I can remember that I think in the first part of the afternoon, two buses were provided and two buses brought some men. And I don't know if they went separate or in a convoy. They left in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me take you back to Acamovic, Colonel Acamovic. Is that a name that you're sure about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we just sat down inside the compound and I had all the time to write his name down. I've got it in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he say anything that restricted the movement of the UN troops to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was in the second meeting we had that day. At the end of the afternoon, at half past 4.00, Akamovic showed up again and told us that there would be a Medevac, medical evacuation, from Bratunac. He told us that the civilian staff could stay with the battalion, that there would be a convoy today from the UNHCR with food in it and we were able to give it to the refugees. It was a very strange situation, of course, because most of the refugees at that moment already left. There never arrived a convoy that day. He ordered us when all the refugees are gone, we have to assemble all the Dutch personnel and we have to stay inside the compound, and the next day, by daylight, there would be a check from the compound if no BiH soldiers stayed behind in the compound. That same moment he took our list we established for him with the local staff and the other personnel, and in my notes I also see that that same afternoon we made a list with 239 names on it from the males who were inside the compound. We made that list and sent it to Tuzla, because we had no possibility to check if everybody arrived in Tuzla. So we asked, give us a list, and one of the -- or several interpreters tried to establish a list for us with all those names from male Muslims inside the compound. We faxed it to Tuzla so they could check if the men would arrive in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was 239 a complete list of all the men --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- inside the compound? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a list from all those men who wanted to be on that list, because not everybody wanted to be on that list and not everybody wanted to give his name. That's what the interpreters told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know one particular Muslim man that was in the compound that you had a concern about? I believe it was Camila Osmanovic's relative.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Camila Osmanovic broke down that day. Her brother was also in the compound. He was the cook of the MSF and he was also on the list from our local staff and would be able to go with us. He was very afraid about what was going to happen, so afraid that he had a rope in his pocket and told me that when Serbs entered the compound, he would hang himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you believe him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believed him, because he really was very afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what time were all the Muslim refugees finally shipped out of the area on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: At about 8.00 in the evening it was the end of the evacuation. Everybody left. At that moment our soldiers went inside the compound. I myself and some other soldiers went to the factories inside of the compound to check if there were no refugees left, if there were no dead bodies or anything else, but we didn't find anything, so at 8.00 everything and everybody was gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on the 14th you were left, I think you said, with 6.000 litres of fuel, and the VRS took 30.000; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And I don't know the exact arrangement which Major Franken made with Jankovic, but I know that a truck went first to the compound, or directly to Bratunac, to support the BSA with the diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the 6.000 that you had, was that enough to fill your vehicles and to get you transported out of the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it must be, because we didn't get any diesel after it, and we got out and we managed, so it was enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And finally, when did DutchBat leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: We finally left at the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's all the questions I have now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I was actually going to interrupt you it so that we could have a break now, and I think this is a good moment for a recess. We will have, therefore, a 20-minute break and then we will resume after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to resume with the cross-examination, but we don't seem to have the witness. Mr. Dubuisson, what is happening? Where is our witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher has gone out to fetch him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness B, are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind you once again that you have to speak slowly. Now you're going to answer questions put do you by the Defence. I believe it is going to be Mr. Petrusic who will cross-examine you. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness B, on the meeting held on the 6th of January, 1995 in Bratunac, you met General Zivanovic, Lieutenant Colonel Vukovic, Major Nikolic, and Major Sarkic. That introduction was done by General Zivanovic, I believe. Did he introduce the said Generals as Generals of the Drina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He just introduced himself as the General Zivanovic, and our predecessors told us he was the Commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You spent some time in the enclave. As of the month of January that year, could you describe the security situation in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the security -- well, for the people over there or for --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I mean the security situation inside the enclave itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we had a rather good security situation inside the enclave. We did not have very big problems. The biggest problems we had were at the borders of the enclave because there was frequent shooting from BSA side to the Muslim side and also from the Muslim side to the BSA side, but indeed the enclave the situation was rather calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of an incident where a patrol of the Dutch Battalion was captured inside the enclave, that is, in the area called the Bandera triangle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not a patrol captured inside the enclave. There were some incidents in that vicinity called the Bandera triangle, and at one moment some patrols were stopped and not allowed to go in there. After that, that problem was solved. We frequently had problems to go there, and the Muslims denied us to go in that triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the reasons why Muslims denied you access to the Bandera triangle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As they told us, and maybe I can show it on the map, the Muslims were afraid that the Milici Brigade would attack this vicinity and the villages in this vicinity. They tried to order us to take a position in the OP Bravo, but we were not allowed to go there and we would not take the position. They ordered us. We would choose it ourselves, and they did not agree with the positions we would like to take. That was one of the reasons for the struggle we had with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: According to the information you had, was the protected zone of Srebrenica completely demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you mean "demilitarised," there were no regular army units, it's yes, but, of course, it was not completely demilitarised because there were men who were in the army before, in the war, and there was still the 8th Operational Group from the BiH in charge and they had a big influence. So it was not completely demilitarised. The only thing we were able to do is deny them to exercise as militaries and they did not; to disarm them, and that was the utmost that we could do and what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge to the effect that during your time there there had been attacks of the forces of the 8th Operational Group against Serb positions, that is, the villages situated outside the protected area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From both sides, as well from the military leaders inside the enclave, as from the Serbian side, we got frequently the information that fights were going on inside the enclave, and at that moment the Muslims accused the Serbs entering the enclave, and outside the enclave the Serbs accusing the Muslims going out and attacking people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about an attack by the 8th Operational Group on the village of Visnjica on the 25th and the 26th of July, 1995 -- I'm sorry, 25th, 26th of June, that is, prior to the fall of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing in my notes, but I can check my other notebook. You said the 25th?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: 25th and 26th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no information that there was an attack. Nothing in -- no invites for meetings with the BiH or the BSA side. I have nothing in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: During your time in the area, did you ever talk to the commanders of the 8th Operational Group in Srebrenica? Because the group was quartered in Srebrenica. And I have a Mr. Moric [sic] in mind, in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name "Moric." The only -- Naser Oric I think you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser Oric. Yes. We had contact with him for the first few months in the enclave, and I think that in March he disappeared. We had no contact with him after the month of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to the events that took place in July 1995. You testified that on the 9th of July, a wounding incident took place, including the Commander van Rensen, who died as a result of the injuries several days later. After that incident did the confidence of the members of the Dutch battalion in respect of Muslim forces subside in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What happened, that when the people on the OP Foxtrot, it was the manning from the OP, and one of the Dutch soldiers died, got into that situation. Of course everybody was informed after that, and when that's on your mind, when you try to use your freedom of movement and act military-wise, as they learned, go backwards with your APC or other vehicles and go forward in another place, and you had an incident like this, and you see when you want to go backward that there are Muslim men, armed Muslim men who maybe want to stop you, well I think at that moment there's something -- there's a change in your mind. But towards the Muslim people, I don't think that the attitude was different than before, because everybody saw it as an incident, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Well, my question did not target the Muslim population as such; I was referring to the Muslim forces. The question, therefore, concerned the Muslim-armed forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no regular armed forces at that moment. Of course, we had our frequent contacts with the Chief of Staff from the 8th OG. Ramiz was acting as the leader of the military people, as far as we knew, in the enclave. Of course, we complained that this situation happened, but it was a civilian, in our view, who killed soldier van Rensen, a Muslim soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of July you went to the PTT building. Could you please tell us whether Muslims, that is, the civilians, made a decision at that time to move into the direction of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had a meeting in the PTT building at 11.00 in the evening. Colonel Karremans told them that there would be airstrikes the next morning, when the ultimatum was not held. Nothing happened further on. When we left the PTT building we saw a lot of men in uniform and in civilian clothes, with arms, going to the north-western part, leaving the town of Srebrenica in the north-western direction, but not in a direction to Potocari, because everybody stayed in Srebrenica. There was a UN compound in the town of Srebrenica, so the anxious people were in the vicinity of that compound. And nobody decided to go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge as to the time when the decision to go to Potocari was reached?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that nobody took a decision to go to Potocari. When the attacks went on on the 11th of July, the refugees collected in the vicinity of the compound of the Bravo Company in Srebrenica. I wasn't outside, but I think, of course, some of them went maybe to Potocari. At 10 minutes past 2.00, according to my notes, there was an airstrike and the mortar shells landed in the compound. That was for us the reason to try, I think, at 12.00 already, to get the people to Potocari, because we had not enough place on the compound to let all the refugees on the compound, and when they would like to go on the UN base, they had to go to Potocari. I did not know at that moment that it was -- that there were so many refugees who would like to go there. But the civilian leaders from the Muslims in the enclave, and also not the military leaders, took that decision. We just told the people, "Well, go to Potocari, because there is no space enough on this compound."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Muslim military forces reached a decision to go to the town of Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there were a real decision to go there. When we left in the night from the 10th to the 11th the PTT building, we saw a lot of armed men going in the north-western direction, leaving the town in that direction. The next day, when I was on the compound of the Bravo Company, I did not see a lot of armed men in that vicinity. Most of them were elderly people, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you identify the units in somewhat more precise terms than simply units of the army of Republika Srpska? And I'm referring to the units who were present in Potocari on the 12th and the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of units it were. I think it was infantry, because they were walking in, I think, the strength of a company in the vicinity of the compound. And they wore Bosnian Serb uniforms, as we saw them several times before when we were at the meetings in Bratunac. That's for me that I think this were the regular Serb forces and infantry, because they walked and they had no vehicles or tanks or APCs with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The meeting that was held in Bratunac in the Fontana Hotel on the 11th of July, around 10.00 p.m., could you please describe the participation of General Krstic in that meeting, or rather the role of General Krstic in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my notes are here and, as I said, at that moment I did not know it was General Krstic. He was announced as a representative; in my view, a representative of the Drina Corps. He was sitting next to General Mladic and looked just what happened and did not do anything: did not speak, did not mix up in the discussions or anything else; just was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did General Zivanovic attend that meeting too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The last time I've seen General Zivanovic was in the first meeting at 8.00, and after that I've never seen General Zivanovic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And you stayed at the meeting until the end, the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness B. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. McCloskey, do you have any questions now on re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a few, and one thing I forgot to ask him the first time

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During the second meeting did any VRS officer or soldiers besides Mladic say anything at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember and see in my notes, there is only General Mladic who was talking to Mr. Mandzic and to Colonel Karremans and making statements. I don't have anything in my notes that somebody else talked or mixed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I asked you earlier to correct the mistake of OP Echo on the map, and were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I put the new OP Echo on the map, over here. It's just at the crossroad over here, and not over there. So it's changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've marked it with a little black "E"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you refer to what is marked as Exhibit 28, which I know you've had a chance to look at, and if you could go to what is tab 2, Exhibit 28/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can he get some help with the ELMO on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise someone on that photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're pointing out the fellow with the more orange face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you go to tab 3, Exhibit 28 -- I believe it's 28/5.1. Excuse me. That is 28/5 and that's fine. 28/5 is fine. You can -- all right. Well, now we're looking at 28/5. Do you recognise that individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Mr. Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a frame that is divided in half but that's the same individual; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If you could go to what is tab 11, Exhibit 28/13. Can you identify those two individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic and Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise where that photo was taken from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think it is in one of the meetings in Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, do you perhaps have any additional questions, because we have heard some new things here. Would you have anything else to ask of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the last photograph, in point of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: During your testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness B said that at the second meeting it was Colonel Jankovic who was sitting to the left of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On this photograph that we just saw, was that the photograph of that second meeting, that is, the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Yes. You may ask the question directly, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure if it's the second meeting. I don't think so because in my view, in the second meeting General Krstic was sitting to the left of General Mladic. I only know the background, the curtains in the Hotel Fontana, so but I think it is in one of the meetings, but I don't know if it is in one of the meetings I joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But on this photograph, is this the left-hand side of General Mladic where Colonel Jankovic is sitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is that to the left of General Mladic? And was this the meeting that cameramen recorded on the video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, the cameras were in the first and the second meeting. I'm not sure if we sat down during the first meeting. I think we did. Now I maybe jumped to a conclusion, and I don't think that's correct. So this must be the first meeting, because in my notes, I am for sure that General Krstic is, in the second meeting, sitting to the left of General Mladic. I don't know what meeting it is. I think this picture is made in the Hotel Fontana, because I think I recognise the curtains behind those two men, but I don't know if it is a picture made in one of the meetings I joined. So I can't confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we saw the video of the -- first meeting and all those present at the meeting were standing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. That's what we saw. I also missed some things which I remembered from that meeting which were not on the tape, so I don't think the whole meeting is on the tape we saw yesterday, because I think we saw a tape for maybe 30 minutes, but some things happened at that first meeting I did not see in the tape. I did not see and hear General Mladic shouting at me and asking if I ordered the close-air support, for example, or to Major Boering. In my mind, I think that also during that meeting we had a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you do not think it is possible that it was as we saw it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we yesterday saw that we were standing and talking. Now you can see, I think, that those two men are sitting on the table. I think it is in the Hotel Fontana. That's all I can say to this picture. I don't know in what meeting this was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. I believe my colleagues also have some questions. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Witness B, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just have some few clarifications to ask you about. When you were asked by the Defence counsel if the protected zone of Srebrenica was completely demilitarised, you said it was not completely demilitarised but they were not having any military exercises. Now, what do you mean by "not completely"? Were people left with pistols, with knives, with cannons? What was that meaning of "not completely"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: We frequently got information from our patrols and there the OPs that there were armed men in the vicinity of our patrols and in the vicinity of our OPs. So that means I can say it was not demilitarised because there were armed men inside the enclave, which is not the same as there are regular parts of armed units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, the people were armed but not armed fighting units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just individuals with arms. When we discovered these kinds of men, we tried to disarm them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did it several times and stocked the weapons, after that, in the weapons collection point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the enclave became demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It became demilitarised more and more. But at the end, of course, we saw that there was so many weapons among the people that we had to conclude, after six months, that we have not been able to find and collect all the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you were speaking about the buses, where men were separated from women and put into -- you mentioned three buses in particular to be sent to Bratunac. People on these buses, were they apparently fighting men or men -- just simple citizens and civilians of all ages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were men from all ages. As I told you, in the crowd of refugees, most of the men who were there were elderly men or boys up to, I think, 17 years old. Most of men between 17 and 50, 60 years were not there. Some of them were there. They were separated just because they were men and not because they were able to recognise them as soldiers. They just wore civilian clothes, and they had to go to the White House to check the names by the BSA and see if they were recognised as soldiers who fought in the war before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there any procedure to make sure that they were soldiers or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only information we had, and then that's what I got confirmed by the UNMO who was in the White House, that men had to give their names. And I don't know in what way they were checked if they were soldiers before or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did they have any military clothes on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said they were accompanied to Bratunac and then your people were not allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to what happened after the people left them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the buses disappeared from our view in the direction of Bratunac. Those three buses were accompanied by a UN vehicle. After that vehicle was stopped, we don't know where the buses went and what happened further on with the men in the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You had no echoes, no people came back from these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only our own soldiers returned and the buses disappeared. I don't know if they disappeared in Bratunac or the same way as the first convoy on their way to Kladanj, because that was also possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you inquire after that where they went or ask for information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we asked for information. We asked several times for information. That was one of our biggest concerns, because we were not allowed to escort all the transports, but we never got an answer on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You also mentioned something and the transcript gave two contradictory answers when you were asked by the Defence counsel if it was a Muslim soldier or civilian who killed, I think, the soldier van Rensen. I think first you said it was a civilian and then it appeared on the transcript that it was not a civilian, it was a soldier. Could you then tell me which one is the right thing? Was he a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a civilian. He was a farmer living in the vicinity of the road over there and living in a house near the dirt road and the main road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, I hope the transcript will be corrected then. Could you tell us something about how it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there any animosity between the people and between him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Or between the troops, your troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our troops had to leave the OP and went with the APC to the road. At that moment, the Muslim population tried to make a blockade on the dirt road to stop the APC, and that's what I mean with freedom of movement. They frequently stopped us because they told us, "You have to go forward. Our enemy and your enemy is in front of you and not backwards." So that was the reason why they tried to stop. I know that they just drove on through the blockade the Muslim people made there, and I'm not sure if it was a shot from a gun or a hand grenade who killed our soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
