utterances.text: And just the last question: When Defence counsel asked you about the meeting at Bratunac in the Fontana Hotel on July 11th at 10.00 p.m., I think, you said that General Krstic was announced as the representative of the Drina Corps. Was he having any, in that meeting, any important contribution in a speech or in a plan or anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was just sitting beside General Mladic and did not say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, did Mladic refer to him as being responsible of any action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing. He was not specifically mentioned by General Mladic. He just was there, as well as a lot of other people were there, and just was sitting there and doing nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But he was announced, you said, as the representative of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The only representative or the top representative?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as a representative of the Drina Corps. That's what I can find in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were there other representatives for the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were, because Major Nikolic was there and Kosoric was there, what I can see in my notes, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How was the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In the representatives of the Drina Corps. Who was the most important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment I did not know the rank of General Krstic. The only one I knew was a Major, was Nikolic, but concerning to the fact that Krstic was sitting beside Mladic he might have been a higher rank, but it he was not announced as a Colonel or a General or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He was not announced as a General? He was or he was not at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not announced as a General. He was just announced as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was he a General, in your knowledge, or was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was in a uniform, and I did not know if he was a General or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness B, do you have an estimate of how many men were in the Potocari compound before the evacuations began, before anybody was put on buses? You mentioned at one point that later on they got a list of the men, I think in the White House, and it was only 239 but not everybody wanted to go on the list, but do you have some estimate of how many men were in the large assembly before the evacuations began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not for sure but I think it's a maximum of 300 inside the compound. Of course, there were outside the compound also a lot of men, but in total I think that men between, and I have to guess, 17 and 70, about of 600.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. During the meetings in the Hotel Fontana that you were present at and General Mladic was there, when General Mladic and Colonel Karremans discussed possible evacuation of the refugees from Potocari, was any distinction made in those discussions between men, women, and children? Was any reference made to the fact that, well, the women and children might be let go but the men might have to be screened or some made prisoners of war exchange, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only thing what was mentioned was that first the wounded, after that elderly people, and then the rest, but not that men should be separated or asked if they were military age or not. That we discovered the next day, the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. Was any mention made in those meetings at all of the men that had gone off with the column that was going off by itself in the direction of Tuzla? Was that the subject of any discussion in the meetings with Mladic that you were present at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only thing was that Mladic asked us to get in contact with the Muslim army to tell them to surrender and to hand over their weapons, and that was the only thing what was mentioned besides what I told you. I think it was the 11th or the 12th that Mladic told me that fights were going on and lots of Muslims and Serbs soldiers were killed in the north-western region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You mentioned at, I think, the second meeting at the Fontana, that General Mladic said that he needed to talk to some of the representatives of the Muslim civilians and, if possible, the military, because the population -- I think this is right -- had to choose where to go. What did you understand that to mean, that the population could decide to stay in Potocari or they could decide where they wanted to be delivered or what was your understanding of what he meant when he said they had to choose where to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he meant that people were free to choose. That's what he told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: To choose between what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: To choose between stay in the enclave, stay in Srebrenica or leave the enclave. And after that leaving, they could choose in several directions. At the end, of course, we saw that there was no choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: There was no choice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody would like to stay, because they were so anxious and there was so many fights going on from the 9th and the 10th that nobody wanted to stay. They just wanted to find a new safe haven to go to. And they had no choice to choose another direction because there was only one thing, get into the bus or the truck like cattle and be brought to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question is: You mentioned that, I think it was Colonel Karremans, who said because the UN escorts had not been allowed to go along with all the buses past Bratunac, that five checkpoints would be set up, which would then report, I guess, whether or not they saw the buses go by. Do you know of any foul-up on that, whether or not there were any subsequent reports back from those checkpoints about the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were allowed to go and escort the convoys. The problem was that when we escorted convoys, irregular troops, as it seemed, stole our vehicles. And when we complained to General Mladic that, in our view, BSA soldiers stole our vehicles, he told us that those were not irregular troops who did it, and he had nothing to say about that. After that we made those four checkpoints -- not five, but four, I think -- and in my view they reported, but I don't have any notes about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness B, I have three questions. My first question: At the meeting held at the Fontana Hotel, where you said General Krstic was present as a representative of the Drina Corps, did you see anything, did you notice anything that by which you could say that he did indeed belong to the Drina Corps; that is, did he have any flashes, any insignia? Did you have any outside signs which could confirm -- by which you could conclude and be certain in your mind that he did indeed belong to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not certain about it, but he sore on his breast the same gold-looking thing as General Zivanovic wore. That was my only reference that it might be a representative of the Drina Corps. That's all. And I think it was his rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, any identification signs, apart from the uniform and apart from that insignia, they were identical with those that General Mladic had, were they, the uniform and the flash or symbol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not for sure if the uniform was the same as General Mladic, because they had light and dark uniforms. I can't say if it was the same. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. Excuse me. But I'm not speaking about General Mladic; I'm talking about General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he wore the same uniform as General Zivanovic, and I think that the gold medal on his breast was the same as those from General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question, Witness B, is as follows: You mentioned that, I believe, on the 12th of July a UN vehicle was stopped while escorting the buses. Could you tell us who was it that intercepted, that stopped that UN vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only information I had was that Lieutenant Versteeg was escorting the buses, that he was stopped by BSA soldiers in Bratunac, and that's all I can say about it. I have not seen the complete report in the OPs room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it was the soldiers of the Serb army which stopped the vehicle; it was the military of the Serb army, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I move on to my third question, which has to do also with the question that Judge Riad has already asked of you. You spoke about the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. Do you have any knowledge -- do you know what is the difference between the demilitarisation and militarisation before it was pronounced a safe haven, a protected zone, and after it was pronounced a protected area? What was the situation before it was pronounced a protected area and after it was pronounced a protected area? What is the difference with regard to the demilitarisation? Do you know what was the situation before and after this proclamation as a protected area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only information I've got, of course, is from our predecessors, that when they came to the enclave, the Canadians were already inside the enclave and started to demilitarise the Muslims inside the enclave. They already gathered a lot of heavy equipment, mortars, heavy machine-guns on wheels, the two tanks, which were stocked in the weapon collection point, and the demilitarisation went on with the 1st and the 2nd Battalion and also with our 3rd Battalion, collecting the weapons and putting them in the weapon collection point. That's the only thing I can tell you about the demilitarisation, because most of the heavy weapons the Muslims had after the war were already collected in the weapon collection point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Witness B. I have no more questions. I should also like to thank my colleagues for questions they asked you. The International Criminal Tribunal wishes to thank you for coming here to testify. I know that you had some hard experience at the time, but we hope that you are recovered now in the calm of your beautiful country. Thank you very much for testifying. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey do we have another witness? I believe now we have worked for one hour. Perhaps we could make a short break now before we begin, because if we do begin, then we shall have to make a break straight away, so perhaps it would be better to make a break now. What do you think, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This other witness is not protected, so we'll take the time to open up the courtroom and get prepared. I do have just a few exhibits to offer into evidence. I can do that now or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if there are some exhibits which need to be adduced, perhaps it would be better to do it now rather than when the other witness is coming in. So in this way we shall not have to make any interruptions; we shall be able to work straight on. So yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First, I would like to offer the tape of meeting 1, Exhibit 39; and secondly, the transcript of that tape, Exhibit 39A; and then also the three photographs identified by the witness: 28/4, 28/5 and 28/13. And that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, do you have any objections to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then these exhibits are admitted. And now we shall make a break, and it will be a 15-minute break, to save some time. So 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that Mr. Cayley is about to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm getting no sound at all, so I will change headsets. I think that's fine. My apology for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it okay now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's perfect. Thank you, Mr. President. With your permission, if I could call the Prosecutor's next witness, which is Mr. Nesib Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please help the witness with the headphones. Can you hear me, Mr. Mandzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're now going to read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, Nesib Mandzic, solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down, Mr. Mandzic. Thank you. Are you comfortable, Mr. Mandzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have translation into Bosnian, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you understand French; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please check the channel. Can you hear me in your language now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I understand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you very much for coming here, Mr. Mandzic. First of all, you are going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Cayley, who is representing the Prosecution. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandzic, I think you were born on the 12th of November, 1962; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think by profession you're a schoolmaster; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, by profession I'm an electrical engineer, but prior to the war I used to work in a secondary school as a teacher in Srebrenica, and also during the war I stayed in the same school, the secondary school in Srebrenica, for a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think at the time of the events with which this court is interested, in July of 1995, you were the head teacher at that school in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Until January of 1993 you were a member of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in January of 1993 I think you left the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you are a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a Bosniak by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. What is your present position within the municipal government in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: At present I'm the president of the Srebrenica municipality. After the legal -- in accordance with the results of the legal elections that took place in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to now take you back to July of 1995, and it's important, as we've already discussed, that you, in response to my questions, you tell the Judges exactly what you heard and saw at the time, how you felt about things, and your perceptions about the feelings about the population in Srebrenica while these events in July of 1995 were taking place. Let us go to the 8th of July, 1995. Where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 8th of July, 1995, I was in Srebrenica, in the central area of the town, in the Petrica Street. This is actually where I lived as a refugee for more than three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, on that day, can you tell the Judges what you saw taking place?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of July, 1995, late in the afternoon I saw columns of people, columns of refugees who had fled a temporary settlement, a temporary shelter that was conducted by the Swedish government in the place called Slapovici. The place was attacked by the artillery of the Serb forces as well as the infantry, and was exposed to an aggression by foot soldiers who entered the said village. They started, according to what those people had said, they started burning down the houses, that is, the temporary shelter that they were using at the time. So on that day in the afternoon, in the street where I used to live, I saw thousands of displaced people who were terrified. There were quite a few elderly people, very weak people, lots of women with small children who were crying. They were in a state of shock. They were looking for some kind of accommodation, some food, clothes, and so on, but that could not be found in Srebrenica in those days, nor could it be found before that, in the previous months. I have to stress that on that day, although a number of columns of refugees were pouring in, the artillery fire of the Serb army never stopped. Shells were falling in the town area, including the places where the refugees were staying, looking for some accommodation that could not be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 4A, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: These individuals, Mr. Mandzic, were they residents originally from the area where the Swedish Housing Project was located or were they from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Mr. Mandzic, if you could answer that question first.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. These people were mostly refugees, displaced persons who, due to aggressive actions of the Serb army, had been expelled from their homes in 1992 and 1993. By a decision of a Swedish government in 1993, some kind of temporary accommodation, a camp, was built for that particular group of refugees. They had come from a number of municipalities, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, and so on. However, the majority of the people who were temporarily accommodated in that housing project were from the area of the Srebrenica municipality, from the inhabited areas that were exposed to the actions of the Serb army units. As a result of those operations, the population was expelled. A number of people had also died in those operations but quite a few of them, therefore, found themselves in Srebrenica. At the beginning of 1993, they were all staying in this shelter project in the village of Slapovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you point to the village of Slapovici on the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Here it is in the upper left corner [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could the exhibit be moved up. I see. And let the record show that the witness is pointing to the bottom left-hand square where it says Slapovici. That is Exhibit 4A.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Let's now move, Mr. Mandzic, to the 9th of the July. First of all, could you look at the map that is behind you, and if you could point to your location on the 9th of July in Srebrenica. Just an approximation would be fine, so the Judges can orient themselves as to where you were on that day.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm showing here [indicates] is the town area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is pointing to an area just below and to the right of where it says "UN Bravo Company" on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E, and in particular where there is a very sharp, hairpin bend in the road going into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. So this is the road leading up to Bratunac, and it goes further down to Potocari, Srebrenica, Zeleni Jadar, south-east, leading up to my birthplace, the village of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandzic. Could you tell the Judges what you saw taking place from your advantage place on the 9th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Aggressive activities of the Serb army continued on the following date, that is, the 9th of July, 1995. The military forces of the Serb army entered the areas inhabited by the people I mentioned. They started setting their houses on fire. As a result of that, the population was forced to flee so as not to end up in the hand of the soldiers of the aggressor. The offensive of the Army of the Republika Srpska continued and moved further to the town area of Srebrenica. On the following day, on the 9th of July, units of the Army of the Republika Srpska continued with their offensive and entered a number of Bosniak villages such as Pusmulici, for example, Bajramovici. These villages are situated less than a one-hour walk from the centre of town. This again complicated the humanitarian situation in the town itself. All of these people needed some kind of accommodation. They needed food, medicines, all of which was impossible to obtain. I personally was convinced, as well as the majority of the population, that due to the fact that Srebrenica had been declared by the United Nations a safe area, that such aggressive acts and offensives of the Republika Srpska army would be stopped and that the humanitarian catastrophe would be prevented. What we feared most was a massacre of the civilian population and we hoped that this would be prevented. Unfortunately, the acts of the Army of the Republika Srpska continued, and in the late afternoon of the 9th of July, the situation was the same. On the next day, the 10th of July, in the evening, units of the Republika Srpska army approached the town area from the south and south-east side. May I show this on the map, please? This would be the area in question [indicated], the area south-east and south of the town. They came very close to the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continue] ... Mr. Mandzic. Could you please demonstrate again where the VRS was on the 10th of July, on that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can show you that. This grey line here [indicated] marks, I believe, the area in question, that is, the boundaries of the safe area. Approximately one or two kilometres away from that, depending on the features of the terrain, prior to the 6th of July, units of the Dutch Battalion had been stationed. They were there as part of UNPROFOR forces. The offensive of the VRS was such that those points had to be moved further on. The Dutch troops had to withdraw. You know very well what the reasons for that were. The Serb forces continued along this line, and on the 10th of July, they reached the first street of the town, the Petrica Street. This is the south-east part of the town. They also came from the direction of the village of Slapovici, from the south side of the town. The VRS army entered the village of Slapovici on the 11th of July. So the VRS practically captured the town from the southern part of the area, and they forced the population to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, just again don't say anything, allow me to speak, because I need to indicate in the record where you're pointing to on the exhibit. On the 10th of July, could you point on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E where the location of the VRS is in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: These are the -- this is where the units were, and this is the area of Zeleni Jadar [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness again is pointing to the area just to the right of where it says "UN Bravo Company" within the area marked as the UN enclave at the point in the road where there is a hairpin bend.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandzic, I'd like to show you some footage, a very short clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the video booth could show Prosecutor's Exhibit 3, the section from -- I think it's 10 seconds in to 31 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Say nothing, Mr. Mandzic, while the video is playing, and then I'll ask you some questions after you've seen that video footage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, if you watch the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. We can stop now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, did you witness those events?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges what you saw and heard on the 10th of July where that event was taking place and what the feelings of the population were at the time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. The video that we just saw was taken on the 10th of July, 1995. As we can see, there were thousands of residents of Srebrenica there. They were all terrified at that time because, as I have already told you, late in the afternoon of that day, the VRS had already entered the first street of the town from the south-east. What I saw there was thousands of terrified people who felt helpless. They were asking for help. They turned to the military representatives of the United Nations, that is, to the Dutch soldiers who were there. They were asking for protection, but they didn't get any answer, any response in terms of protection. On that night, approximately 40.000 people in Srebrenica could have no sleep at all. I couldn't sleep either, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, could you just indicate on the map behind you the location of that large group of people that we've just seen on the video?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This gathering took place in front of the compound of the Vezionica factory in Srebrenica, and it is marked on the map here [indicated]. It's this area that I'm pointing now [indicated].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is pointing to the blue square marked "UN Bravo Company" within the Srebrenica enclave on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, let's move ahead in time to the 11th of July, 1995. You were still in the town of Srebrenica. Can you tell the Judges what you saw and heard on that day?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about the urban area of Srebrenica, from that area more than half of the population had been expelled, forced out due to the military activities of the VRS, who, as early as the 10th of July, started setting Bosniak houses on fire in the Petrica Street. They were still firing from infantry weapons and so on. On the 11th of July, after 11.00 a.m., the situation got further complicated, because the VRS opened fire from their artillery, targeting the population itself and opening fire on the area where the population had gathered on the 10th of July, late in the afternoon. I was very close to the area, some 70 metres as the crow flies, on the other side of the street. I was standing next to a building, and I could hear very well the sound of shells, artillery shells coming in. Immediately after that, I would actually see the shell fall on the group of between 5.000 and 10.000 refugees who were staying there, expecting some kind of response from the UNPROFOR forces. They somehow felt safer in the vicinity of UNPROFOR. Immediately after this shell had fallen, I happened to see a terrible scene. I saw a column of smoke rising from the spot where the people had gathered. I heard screams, moans. There were some wounded people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On that day, I think there was an expectation that there would be airstrikes. How did the population in and around the UN Bravo Company react to these rumours?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is true that we expected the NATO air force to prevent the capture of the enclave and the exodus of the population. Until 11.00 a.m. those were some unreliable pieces of information that people accepted in those situations, as a drowning man is looking for a straw to hold on to to save himself. So on that day for us, the only possibility, the only way out was for this type of action. Only in this way could the VRS be stopped. In the afternoon of the 11th of July, I could see, as far as I can remember, two aeroplanes in the skies above Srebrenica, which did drop several bombs on, I believe, Serbian artillery positions. And as far as I can remember the area in question was south-east. It was here [indicates], but it's not indicated on the map. There is a feature there called Kvarc, and I believe that that was the area where a radio transmitter was stationed. My feeling is that this was -- this area was the target of the NATO Air Force. At any rate, this was close to the boundary of the safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on in time, Mr. Mandzic. The population started to move towards Potocari. Can you tell the Judges when that happened and why it happened?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: The population was forced to move. This happened on the 11th of July, around 4.00 p.m. The residents of the town started to move towards Potocari. They were actually forced to leave the last part of the safe area, because the VRS had continued with its offensive activities. So the population was actually being pushed from the area. They couldn't go back. They couldn't go back to the enclave itself, because everybody could see Bosniak houses on fire at that time. So in view of the situation, in view of the fear and feeling of helplessness, residents started to move towards Potocari, which was the last safe haven in the area, that is, the command of the Dutch battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, are you aware as to whether or not any senior member of the population, or members of the population, took a decision that the population would move to Potocari from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: It was no higher representative who would be inviting people to head for Potocari. It was all civilian population and they all thought about Potocari. The majority of the civilians thought about Potocari, because the major part of the enclave had already been physically taken by the troops of the VRS and there was nowhere else to go. We could only withdraw by a couple of kilometres further on towards the Dutch compound at Potocari. So the passage of the civilian population through the area, even those areas that were inhabited by Bosniaks before the war, but they had been taken by the armed forces of the Republika Srpska, so it was impossible to go through those places. Both the Serb artillery and infantry fire were targeting the population directly, and it seemed that their objective was to kill as many civilians as possible, to sow as much panic, to sow as much chaos amongst them. And I can also corroborate by saying the following: On the 11th of July, I happened to be in the column of the civilian population on the road to Potocari. At that time the Serb artillery fired at us. From the neighbouring hills we could clearly see that there were -- they could see that there were tens of thousands of refugees who were on their way to Potocari, to the Dutch battalion. But they were so aggressive that they simply opened direct fire on this stream of refugees which was several kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, try and speak more slowly, because there are interpreters that have got to keep up with you. I know it's difficult to speak about these events, but stay calm, and we'll get through your testimony as quickly as I can. Let's move to the evening of the 11th of July, 1995. Where do you find yourself?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I found myself at Potocari, or to be more accurate, within the compound of the 11 of March Factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you point on the map that's behind you the approximate location of where you were on the evening of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is pointing at Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E, to the red-coloured triangle, just below where it's marked "UN base," within the area marked as the Srebrenica enclave. Can you tell the Judges the scene on the evening of the 11th of July in and around the UN compound at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The scene was hair-raising. Something about 25.000 of those expellees [Realtime transcript read in error "ex-police"] were crowding in a very small, in a very tight space. They tried to find some accommodation in some ancient factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, if you could stop there. There's a mistake in the transcript and then you said the scene was hair-raising and then you said, "Something about 25.000 of those..." Twenty-five thousand of whom?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: The expellees, the expelled refugees, Bosniak people who had been expelled from the largest part of the enclave, because only a minor part of the enclave was surviving, and that was Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please continue with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: At that very small space of perhaps less than one kilometre square, there were some 25.000 expelled. Most of them were women with small children, elderly and emaciated people. We were all without food or water or medicines or clothing or footwear, accommodation, or anything. We expected that the International Community would give us protection, fearing the worst from the Bosnian Serb army, and indeed I do remember that 11th of July, sometime around 2100, the Bosnian Serb army launched an operation. As far as I can remember, they opened artillery fire at this crowd, this multitude of people forced into that space.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see the artillery firing?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, they fired over my head, over the heads of 25.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how far away they were, the VRS artillery, when they were firing at this huge multitude of people?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Some 300 to 500 meters. From different places, so I say it was 300 meters was the closest and 500 meters was perhaps the site furthest away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did the population react to this artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: We all tried to find some shelter, but there was none, so we simply threw ourselves down on the asphalt, somewhere in the street, that is, on the road from Potocari to Bratunac, because they couldn't find any shelter whatsoever. So panic again started, screaming, and so --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know of any deaths or injuries that were caused by that artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: As soon as this artillery fire stopped, the Dutch battalion called me, and so that night I could not really hear if there had been any wounded, because that night, between the 11th and the 12th, I spent in the camp of the Dutch soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And now we very neatly move on to the next part of your testimony. I think at about 9.30 that evening you were called by a representative of the Dutch battalion to act as a representative of the civilian population. Could you tell the Judges about that, please.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime around half past 9.00 that evening, between the 11th and the 12th of July, I was asked over the PA system to report to the Dutch battalion command. So I went to the commander of the Dutch battalion. I did not know him before that, nor did I know any of their officers, except Major Boering, who used to come to the secondary school. So after I was introduced to the commander of the Dutch battalion and his officers, the Dutch battalion commander, showing major concern, major anxiety, and sounding very pessimistic, said that, as he saw the situation, the Dutch soldiers, and he as a commander, could do very little at that particular point in time to help all those population who had gathered force in Potocari; and also, as the commander said, the situation was also highly unfavourable for Dutch soldiers as well. According to the commander of the Dutch battalion, the only way out would be the negotiations with the army of the Republika Srpska, and as far as I can recall, that the army of the Republika Srpska was demanding the Dutch officers to incorporate the Bosnian side in the negotiations. I commented, I said that I was not an official representative of the civilian authorities in the municipality of Srebrenica, and I said so to the Dutch commander, and that I therefore had no authority to represent anyone in a situation which was as complex as that one. And the Dutch battalion commander said, "Yes, we do know that, but the situation is very dramatic. So come on behalf of these expelled people, because they, and we, and everybody, needs help." And having been given a promise by the Dutch battalion commander that if I joined the negotiations, that I would be -- that my requests, that my conditions would be supported: that is, to begin with, to stop firing at the civilian population, to resolve the disastrous humanitarian situation; that is, to supply the population with food, water, other arms of hygiene and so on and so forth. And after I was promised that, on the 11th of July, I set off for the negotiations in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, before we get to Bratunac, I want to go back to the conversation that you had with the Dutch commander. Did the Dutch commander, Colonel Karremans, state to you what General Mladic had said to him about the refugees in and around Potocari and about his own soldiers that were, in fact, hostages at that time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I know that the Dutch battalion commander said that the situation was also highly unpropitious for the Dutch soldiers who were on the UNPROFOR mission in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he state to you whether Mladic had said anything about the safety of the civilian population in and around Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I do not know really what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on. You then went with the Dutch officers to Bratunac. How did you feel at that time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Right below the camp of the Dutch soldiers in Potocari was the checkpoint of the VRS, and it was right there at this first checkpoint that we were stopped. And they asked who was I, I mean the soldiers of the army of the Republika Srpska, and it was all in rather threatening tones. And even as I was on the road, I already was quite fearful. I didn't know what might happen to me. And I was thinking about the worst possible outcome, that I might be arrested and forced to -- I don't know what. But I thought one thing, and one thing only, and that was to try, to try to do my best on behalf of the population which was left completely without any protection, because I could really see that the enclave was being taken and that an area which had been protected by the United Nations was being taken. On the other hand, the United Nations kept silent. And even the mildest type of reaction that they could have done, they could have sent in teams of the International Red Cross at least there, or the UNHCR, to try to mitigate, to allay, to ease this difficult, this horrible situation, especially the humanitarian disaster. And in such good faith, to try to alleviate the suffering of the population, is that I went to Bratunac, but I was really frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point we're going to move into some video evidence, and if it's your wish, we might take a short break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley. Very well. We shall then make a break, 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, if we can just reorient the Court where we were. You left the Potocari compound at about 2200 hours on the night of the 11th of July, and you find yourself with members of the Dutch Battalion driving towards Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies. You're quite correct. Towards Bratunac. What time did you arrive in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Within approximately ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where did you go within Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: We went to the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think it was there that you attended a meeting with members of the VRS and the Bosnian Serb civilian authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At this point, Mr. President, the Office of the Prosecutor would like to play a video of that meeting. That video is a new exhibit. It's Exhibit 4D. My apologies. It's Exhibit 40. It's Exhibit 40. There are three transcripts of that meeting, in English, French, and in B/C/S. I would ask that the interpreters please remain silent during the video, because I think it's important for the Court to get a sense of that meeting and the tone and intonation of the individuals who speak at that meeting. So if you don't mind, Your Honours, following in that transcript. It's an accurate transcript of what was said at that meeting. There are also some external noises that are actually quite important that need to be heard, and they would not be heard if the interpreters were speaking over the soundtrack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay. We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the video booth could please play Exhibit 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, first an obvious question but for the purposes of legal foundation of the video: Is this a video recording of parts of the meeting that happened on the 11th of July, 1995, in the evening at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it reflects the essential part of what was being discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are there parts of the meeting that are not on that video recording?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are certain parts. For example, a part when General Mladic addressed me in a threatening way, speaking about the genocide committed against the Serbian people. He also referred to the fate of the Bosniaks in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he blamed high-ranking Bosniak politicians for that. He said, General Mladic, "You see, they're unable to help you now, neither Ganic, nor his people."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges who Ganic was? Who was Mladic referring to?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Professor Dr. Ejub Ganic was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina as of 1992 until 1995. It was a collective body, leadership that was in charge of the community as was Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall anything else that General Mladic said at that meeting which is not on that video recording?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. At several points, General Mladic mentioned the fact that the VRS had completely defeated the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was referring to the areas around Tuzla or Sarajevo. I'm not sure. He wasn't very explicit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've taken a number of stills off the video which I'd like to show the witness because that's the easiest way of having him identify various individuals, rather than go back through the video which will be a very lengthy process. So we if we would make available, please, Prosecutor's Exhibits 41 to 46 and also 48, please, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: May I add something, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course you can, Mr. Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: According to my recollection from that first meeting, most of the people present were high-ranking officers of the VRS, and I did not notice representatives of the civilian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're now referring to the meeting on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Yes, the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the Exhibit 41 could be placed on the ELMO, please. We'll do this very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 41. Can you identify this individual, please, Mr. Mandzic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the commander of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Karremans. I don't know whether my pronunciation is correct, and I don't know whether this is his last name or first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is just fine, Mr. Mandzic. Exhibit 42. Who is this individual, Mr. Mandzic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: The individual here is Petar, the interpreter. Today he's working as an interpreter for the UN in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the area of Zvornik, and you can often see him in Bratunac and Srebrenica. He's working for the IPTF mission there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness can be shown Exhibit 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is an officer of the VRS. As far as I can remember, he was the one who mentioned the towns of Vlasenica, Rogatica, and Han Pijesak, and this is how I concluded that he must have been from that area or that the area in question was his zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall where he was sitting during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: He was sitting next to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 44. Can you identify that individual in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: General of the VRS, the Commander of the VRS, General Mladic, Ratko Mladic, whom in those days, from the 11th until the 21st of July, I saw four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit 45. Do you recognise this individual?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. General Krstic, who is sitting here on my left. On the 11th of July, General Krstic was introduced by his commander, General Ratko Mladic. He also introduced other officers from his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you please identify. You said that General Krstic is sitting here on my left. Could you point across to the person that you recognise as General Krstic in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's sitting on my left. He's wearing a blue shirt and a tie [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show, Mr. President that the witness has identified the accused, General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And where was General Krstic sitting at this meeting on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Next to General Mladic. As far as I can remember, he was sitting on his right-hand side. There was another meeting where he also sat next to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when you say, Mr. Mandzic, that he was sitting on General Mladic's right-hand side, you are saying that as if you were General Mladic, from General Mladic's perspective?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, and according to my recollection, at the table where we were sitting in the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac, General Krstic was sitting on General Mladic's right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Am I any closer in my description now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's fine, and I think the video was very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandzic, what is this object which I think is in fact in front of you on the video?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: This is a board carrying the inscription, first of all, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; underneath, Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica; and at the bottom, in the last line, Srebrenica. As I have said, this was on the municipal building, on the town hall, and it marked the centre of the municipal administration. And General Mladic showed me this inscription and he asked me whether I could recognise it, and I said, "Yes, I do recognise it."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This broken sign that was placed before you, at the time what significance did you feel that it had that it was placed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: It was a clear message that the enclave had been taken, that is, that the protected area had been taken; a clear message that the civilian population which had lived there could no longer stay there; a clear message that in the days to come, the operations of the VRS would target other enclaves; that is, first of all, most of the population in those enclaves, such as Gorazde, Bihac, and Sarajevo. And it was also a clear message that that could well be the end of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the order it represented. And that after that, the army of the Republika Srpska would make it possible to create a mono-ethnic state product without the participation of the other two constituent ethnicities, Croats and Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandzic. On the video, on the soundtrack of the video, near the beginning, there were some screams that were heard. Can you tell the Judges what those screams were and how you interpreted that at the time of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. One could hear a pig screaming, or rather that night, or at that moment, I thought that perhaps some Serb soldiers were celebrating the taking over of the protected area and the expulsion of Bosniaks. And to be quite honest, that was the first thing that I thought of. I did not attribute any particular significance to the slaughter of that pig or the festivity. But after all these years, I still remember those screams. It was a message that the same procedure would be applied, the same method, to also bleed the Bosniaks, the Muslim Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Mandzic, can you tell the Judges the atmosphere at that meeting, how you felt in front of General Krstic, General Mladic, these VRS officers.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Very afraid, very ashamed, defenceless, especially when I noticed that the commander of the Dutch battalion could not properly voice, articulate the needs of the expelled population, civilian population. And also when General Mladic interrupted me when I requested -- when I asked General Mladic and the commander of the Dutch battalion whether all the needs of the civilian population and the status of the enclave had been reported to the civilian and military structures of the International Community. And when General Mladic cut me short and would not allow me to continue speaking about that need, his tone was threatening, he focused his eyes at me, he stared at me. I think he wanted to frighten me. And he frequently used the word that the fate of my people, the people that I originated from, was in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. Mandzic, I just want to address with you some of the language that was used by General Mladic at the meeting, and this is on page 8 of the English transcript, line 3, when Mladic states: "I need to have a clear position of the representatives of your people on whether you want to survive, stay, or disappear, and I am prepared to receive a delegation tomorrow of responsible people from the Muslim side here, at 1000 hours, with whom I can discuss the salvation of your people from the enclave, the former enclave of Srebrenica." How did you interpret this when you heard this?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Major anguish, scared, really scared. I really was very concerned what would happen to those several dozen thousand of refugees, because General Mladic repeatedly said "vanish or survive." And he also used the word "the former enclave." And I responded that same moment, because indeed the army of the Republika Srpska, or rather the command of the VRS, had decided to deport the Bosniak population by hook or by crook. And that word, "to survive or to vanish," it really frightened me, because he seemed to be announcing already some steps, some measures which had little to do with civilisation or with humanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall him saying to you, "Do you understand me, Nesib? The future of your people is in your hands"?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes, I remember that. I do indeed. I do not know what General Mladic wanted from me. He wanted to demonstrate the force of his own, of the power of his army on a civilian, saying that I would be representing 30.000 other people. But yes, indeed, during that meeting and during that night, from what I heard from General Mladic, I was very pessimistic as to the positive, as to the favourable outcome for those 30.000 expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think he finally said to you, when you advised him that you were an accidental representative, he stated, "That is your problem. Bring people who can secure the surrender of weapons and save your people from destruction." And that, I think, was the end of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic was well aware that there were between 25 and 30.000 of those expellees in Potocari and that they were, by and large, women, small children, elderly, sick people, and that there were no armed groups amongst them. He also knew that his units were a few steps away from that expelled population, about a hundred or perhaps 200 meters, and that during the night they would reach that expelled population of -- those units of the VRS would reach that population. He knew that, but insisting by saying, by pointing out to me that the fate of the Bosnian people was in my hands. I believe he wanted to discourage me in voicing any other requests in the first place, to treat that expelled population humanely, not to turn it into a ghetto. And that indeed was a ghetto for all those people. I can confirm it now, and I was quite clear then, that it had been a planned operation of the VRS for those several days to force the civilian population to leave their homes, to leave all their belongings behind, and to be forced into a small place, into a small compound, such as Potocari, and that the control over that area should be taken over by the units of the VRS and which would then turn it into a ghetto.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At what time did you leave this meeting on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I think it was sometime between 11.00 and half past eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where did you go when you left?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I left the meeting together with the officers of the Dutch Battalion, and I spent that night with them at their headquarters in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you wish, I can move on to the 12th of July or we can finish here, however you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Cayley, there is still yet another exhibit, which is 48, which I think was not shown the witness. Would you please do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. You're quite right. If the witness could be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after that we could, yes, adjourn for the day. But now I believe we could really benefit from this occasion and show the witness that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Exhibit 48 would be placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, do you recognise this individual?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC
utterances.text: I do. Yes. This is Major Boering, if I'm pronouncing his name well, the liaison officer of the Dutch Battalion. He came several times to the secondary school where I worked, where I was the principal, and I repeatedly informed Major Boering about the needs of the pupils in that school, that they needed various school aids and appliances because we did not have that and we could not get any school aids because the convoy couldn't enter Srebrenica because it was prevented from doing so by the units of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall adjourn and tomorrow we shall resume at half past nine. Until tomorrow then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: at 2.30 p.m. to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of March, 2000 at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Closed session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of Trial Chamber]
